paragraphs: I am well aware of the difficulties this part of my subject involves. Every statement I am about to make may clash, on some point or other, with the feelings of the different parties that divide my country. Even so, I will speak my mind with complete openness.

In Europe we have trouble judging the true character and the more lasting tendencies of democracy, because two opposing principles exist side by side there, and we cannot tell what belongs to the principles themselves and what to the passions they set against each other. America is different. There the people rules without any obstacle, with no dangers to fear and no injuries to avenge. In America democracy follows its own free inclinations; its course is natural and its activity unrestrained. The United States therefore offers the best opportunity for studying its real character. And no people has a more vital interest in this inquiry than the French nation, which is driven blindly onward by a daily, irresistible impulse toward a state of things that may turn out despotic or republican, but will certainly be democratic.

I have already noted that universal suffrage has been adopted in all the States of the Union. It therefore operates among populations that hold very different positions on the social scale. I have had the chance to observe its effects in different places, and among peoples who are almost strangers to one another in language, religion, and way of life: in Louisiana as in New England, in Georgia and in Canada. I have noticed that universal suffrage is far from producing in America either all the good or all the evil consequences that people in Europe assign to it, and that its effects differ very widely from those usually attributed to it.
Choice of the People, and Instinctive Preferences of the American Democracy

In the United States the ablest men are rarely placed at the head of affairs — The reason for this peculiarity — The envy that the lower orders of France feel toward the higher classes is not a French sentiment but a purely democratic one — Why the most distinguished men in America so often withdraw from public affairs.

Many people in Europe tend to believe without saying so, or to say without believing, that one of the great advantages of universal suffrage is that it puts the direction of public affairs in the hands of men who deserve the public’s confidence. They admit that the people cannot govern itself, but they assert that it is always sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of the State, and that it instinctively picks out those who share its good intentions and are best fit to hold supreme authority. I confess that what I observed in America does not agree with these opinions at all. When I arrived in the United States I was surprised to find so much distinguished talent among the governed and so little among the heads of the government. It is a well-established fact that today the ablest men in the United States are very rarely placed at the head of affairs, and it must be acknowledged that this has come about as democracy has overstepped all its former limits. The breed of American statesmen has clearly declined remarkably over the last fifty years.

Several causes may explain this phenomenon. No matter how great the effort, it is impossible to raise the intelligence of the people above a certain level. However easy it becomes to acquire information, however many simple methods and cheap forms of knowledge are on offer, the human mind can never be instructed and educated without devoting a considerable amount of time to those goals.

The greater or lesser possibility of living without labor is therefore the necessary boundary of intellectual improvement. This boundary lies farther off in some countries and closer in others, but it must exist somewhere as long as the people must work to obtain the means of physical subsistence — that is, as long as it keeps its popular character. It is therefore just as hard to imagine a State in which all the citizens are very well informed as one in which they are all wealthy; the two difficulties may be seen as correlative. It is easy to grant that the mass of citizens sincerely want to promote the welfare of their country. Indeed, one may even allow that the lower classes are less swayed by considerations of personal interest than the higher orders. But it is always more or less impossible for them to discern the best means of reaching the end they sincerely desire. Long and patient observation, together with a multitude of different ideas, is needed to form a just estimate of the character of a single individual. Can we suppose that the common people can succeed in an inquiry that misleads even the penetration of genius? The people has neither the time nor the means that an investigation of this kind requires; it forms its conclusions hastily, from a superficial look at the most prominent features of a question. Hence it often goes along with the clamor of a charlatan who knows the secret of stimulating its tastes, while its truest friends frequently fail in their efforts.

Moreover, democracy lacks not only the soundness of judgment needed to select men who really deserve its confidence; it also has neither the desire nor the inclination to find them. It cannot be denied that democratic institutions have a very strong tendency to foster the feeling of envy in the human heart. This is not so much because they give everyone the means of rising to the level of any fellow citizen, as because those means perpetually disappoint the people who use them. Democratic institutions awaken and nourish a passion for equality that they can never entirely satisfy. Complete equality slips out of the people’s grasp at the very moment it thinks it has caught it, and “flies,” as Pascal says, “with eternal flight.” The people is excited by the pursuit of an advantage that is all the more precious because it is neither remote enough to be unknown nor near enough to be enjoyed. The lower orders are stirred by the chance of success and irritated by its uncertainty. They pass from the enthusiasm of pursuit to the exhaustion of failure, and finally to the bitterness of disappointment. Whatever rises above their own level appears to them an obstacle to their desires, and there is no kind of superiority, however legitimate, that they do not find irksome.

It has been supposed that the secret instinct that leads the lower orders to keep their superiors as far as possible from the direction of public affairs is peculiar to France. This is an error. The tendency I mean belongs not to any particular nation but to democratic institutions in general. Special political circumstances may have heightened it, but it comes from a deeper cause.

In the United States the people is not inclined to hate the superior classes of society, but it is not very favorably disposed toward them either, and it carefully excludes them from the exercise of authority. It does not fear distinguished talents, but it is rarely captivated by them, and it gives its approval very sparingly to those who have risen without popular support.

While the natural tendencies of democracy lead the people to reject the most distinguished citizens as its rulers, those citizens are just as inclined to withdraw from a political career in which it is almost impossible to keep one’s independence or to advance without degrading oneself. Chancellor Kent has stated this view very frankly. Speaking with great praise of that part of the Constitution which empowers the Executive to nominate the judges, he says: “It is indeed probable that the men who are best fitted to discharge the duties of this high office would have too much reserve in their manners, and too much austerity in their principles, for them to be returned by the majority at an election where universal suffrage is adopted.” Such were the opinions printed without contradiction in America in the year 1830!
I consider it sufficiently demonstrated that universal suffrage is by no means a guarantee of wisdom in the people’s choice, and that, whatever its advantages may be, this is not one of them.

Causes Which May Partly Correct These Tendencies of the Democracy — Great dangers have opposite effects on peoples and on individuals — Why so many distinguished men stood at the head of affairs in America fifty years ago — The influence that the intelligence and the customs of the people exercise on its choice — The example of New England — The States of the Southwest — The influence of certain laws on the people’s choice — Election by an elected body — Its effect on the composition of the Senate.

When a State is threatened by serious dangers, the people often succeeds in choosing the citizens best able to save it. It has been observed that people rarely stay at their usual level when facing very critical circumstances: they rise above their ordinary condition or sink below it, and the same happens to whole nations. Extreme perils sometimes quench a people’s energy instead of stimulating it; they excite its passions without directing them, and instead of clearing its perception they confuse it. The Jews flooded the smoking ruins of their temple with the slaughter of the remnant of their army. But it is more common, for nations as for individuals, to see extraordinary virtues arise from the very nearness of danger. Great characters then stand out, as buildings hidden by the darkness of night are lit up by the glare of a fire. In those dangerous times genius no longer holds back from entering the arena, and the people, alarmed by the perils of its situation, buries its envious passions in a brief oblivion. Great names may then come out of the ballot box.

I have already observed that the American statesmen of today are far inferior to those who stood at the head of affairs fifty years ago. This is as much a result of circumstances as of the country’s laws. When America was struggling in the high cause of independence to throw off the yoke of another country, and was about to usher a new nation into the world, the spirits of its inhabitants were raised to the height that their great efforts required. In this general excitement the most distinguished men were ready to anticipate the community’s needs, and the people clung to them for support and placed them at its head. But events of this magnitude are rare, and our judgment must be formed from the ordinary course of affairs.

If passing events sometimes act as a check on the passions of democracy, the intelligence and the customs of the community exercise an influence that is no less powerful and far more lasting. This is extremely noticeable in the United States.

In New England the education and the liberties of the communities grew out of the moral and religious principles of their founders. Where society has gained enough stability to hold certain maxims and keep settled habits, the lower orders are accustomed to respect intellectual superiority and to submit to it without complaint, although they disregard all the privileges that wealth and birth have introduced among human beings. The democracy in New England therefore chooses more judiciously than it does elsewhere.

But as we move toward the South, to those States where the constitution of society is more recent and less firm, where education is less widespread, and where the principles of morality, religion, and liberty are less happily combined, we see the talents and virtues of those in authority growing steadily rarer.

Finally, when we reach the new Southwestern States, where the constitution of society dates only from yesterday and consists of a jumble of adventurers and speculators, we are amazed at the people who hold public authority. We are led to ask what force, independent of the legislation and of the men who direct it, can protect the State and make society flourish.

There are, however, certain laws of a democratic nature that help to correct, to some extent, the dangerous tendencies of democracy. On entering the House of Representatives in Washington, one is struck by the unrefined demeanor of that great assembly. The eye often fails to find a famous man within its walls. Its members are almost all obscure individuals whose names call nothing to mind: they are mostly village lawyers, tradesmen, or even people from the lower classes of society. In a country where education is very widespread, it is said that the people’s representatives do not always know how to write correctly.

A few yards from this spot is the door of the Senate, which holds within a small space a large share of the celebrated men of America. Hardly anyone in it fails to bring to mind an active and illustrious career. The Senate is made up of eloquent advocates, distinguished generals, wise magistrates, and statesmen of note, whose speeches would at any time do honor to the most remarkable parliamentary debates in Europe.

What, then, causes this strange contrast, and why are the ablest citizens found in one assembly rather than the other? Why is the first body remarkable for its lack of refinement and its poverty of talent, while the second seems to have a monopoly on intelligence and sound judgment? Both assemblies come from the people; both are chosen by universal suffrage; and no one in America has so far claimed that the Senate is hostile to the interests of the people. What, then, causes so startling a difference? The only reason that seems to me an adequate explanation is that the House of Representatives is elected directly by the populace, while the Senate is elected by elected bodies. The whole body of citizens names the legislature of each State, and the Federal Constitution turns these legislatures into so many electoral bodies, which choose the members of the Senate. Senators are thus elected by an indirect application of universal suffrage. The legislatures that name them are not aristocratic or privileged bodies exercising the vote in their own right; they are chosen by the totality of the citizens, they are generally elected every year, and new members can constantly be chosen who will use their electoral rights in accordance with the wishes of the public. But passing the people’s authority through an assembly of chosen men makes an important change in it, by refining its judgment and improving the forms it takes. Men chosen in this way accurately represent the majority of the nation that governs them, but they represent the elevated thoughts current in the community and the tendencies that prompt its nobler actions, rather than the petty passions that disturb it or the vices that disgrace it.

We can already foresee the time when the American Republics will have to use the plan of election by an elected body more often in their system of representation, or else run no small risk of perishing miserably on the shoals of democracy.

And here I have no hesitation in confessing that I regard this particular system of election as the only means of bringing the exercise of political power within reach of all classes of the people. Those thinkers who see this institution as the exclusive weapon of one party, and those who on the other hand fear to use it, seem to me to make an equally great error in either case.
Influence Which the American Democracy Has Exercised on the Laws Relating to Elections

When elections are rare, they expose the State to a violent crisis — When they are frequent, they keep up a degree of feverish excitement — The Americans have preferred the second of these two evils — Mutability of the laws — The opinions of Hamilton and Jefferson on this subject.

When elections recur at long intervals, the State is exposed to violent agitation each time they take place. Parties strain every nerve to win a prize so rarely within their reach, and since the harm is almost irreparable for the candidates who fail, the consequences of their disappointed ambition may prove disastrous. If, on the other hand, the legal struggle can be repeated within a short time, the defeated parties are patient. But when elections occur frequently, their recurrence keeps society in a perpetual state of feverish excitement and gives public affairs a constant instability.

Thus, on the one hand, the State is exposed to the perils of revolution, and on the other to perpetual change. The first system threatens the very existence of the government; the second is an obstacle to any steady and consistent policy. The Americans have preferred the second of these evils to the first. But instinct led them to this conclusion much more than reason did, for a taste for variety is one of the characteristic passions of democracy. In this way an extraordinary mutability has been introduced into their legislation. Many Americans regard the instability of their laws as a necessary consequence of a system whose general results are beneficial. But no one in the United States pretends to deny that this instability exists, or to argue that it is not a great evil.

After demonstrating the usefulness of a power that could prevent, or at least impede, the passing of bad laws, Hamilton adds: “It might perhaps be said that the power of preventing bad laws includes that of preventing good ones, and may be used to the one purpose as well as to the other. But this objection will have little weight with those who can properly estimate the mischiefs of that inconstancy and mutability in the laws which form the greatest blemish in the character and genius of our governments.” (Federalist, No. 73.) And again, in No. 62 of the same work, he observes: “The facility and excess of law-making seem to be the diseases to which our governments are most liable. . . . The mischievous effects of the mutability in the public councils arising from a rapid succession of new members would fill a volume: every new election in the States is found to change one-half of the representatives. From this change of men must proceed a change of opinions and of measures, which forfeits the respect and confidence of other nations, poisons the blessings of liberty itself, and diminishes the attachment and reverence of the people toward a political system which betrays so many marks of infirmity.”

Jefferson himself, the greatest Democrat that the democracy of America has yet produced, pointed out the same evils. “The instability of our laws,” he said in a letter to Madison, “is really a very serious inconvenience. I think that we ought to have obviated it by deciding that a whole year should always be allowed to elapse between the bringing in of a bill and the final passing of it. It should afterward be discussed and put to the vote without the possibility of making any alteration in it; and if the circumstances of the case required a more speedy decision, the question should not be decided by a simple majority, but by a majority of at least two-thirds of both houses.”

Public Officers Under the Control of the Democracy in America — The simple exterior of American public officers — No official costume — All public officers are paid — Political consequences of this system — No public career exists in America — The result of this.

Public officers in the United States mingle with the crowd of citizens; they have no palaces, no guards, and no ceremonial costumes. This simple exterior of the people in authority is connected not only with peculiarities of the American character but with the fundamental principles of that society. In the democracy’s view, a government is not a benefit but a necessary evil. Public officers must be granted a certain degree of power, for they would be of no use without it. But the outward show of authority is by no means indispensable to the conduct of affairs, and it needlessly offends the sensibilities of the public. The officers themselves know well that they enjoy their superiority over their fellow citizens, which comes from their authority, only on condition of putting themselves on a level with the whole community through their manners. A public officer in the United States is invariably civil, accessible to everyone, attentive to all requests, and obliging in his replies. I was pleased by these features of a democratic government, and I was struck by the manly independence of the citizens, who respect the office more than the officer and are less attached to the emblems of authority than to the man who bears them.

I am inclined to believe that the influence costumes really have, in an age like ours, has been greatly exaggerated. I never noticed that a public officer in America was any less respected while discharging his duties because nothing external set off his own merit. On the other hand, it is very doubtful that a special dress contributes to the respect public figures ought to have for their own positions, at least when they are not otherwise inclined to respect them. When a magistrate (and in France such cases are not rare) indulges his petty wit at the prisoner’s expense, or mocks the plight of an offender, it would be good to strip him of his robes of office and see whether he recalls some part of the natural dignity of mankind once he is reduced to the clothes of a private citizen.

A democracy may, however, allow a certain show of magisterial pomp and dress its officers in silk and gold without seriously compromising its principles. Privileges of this kind are temporary; they belong to the position and are distinct from the individual. But if public officers are not uniformly paid by the State, public duties must be entrusted to men of wealth and independence, who form the basis of an aristocracy; and if the people still keeps its right of election, that election can only be made from a certain class of citizens. When a democratic republic makes unpaid the offices that were formerly paid, we may safely believe that the State is moving toward monarchical institutions. And when a monarchy begins to pay officers who had until then been unpaid, it is a sure sign that it is approaching a despotic or a republican form of government. In my opinion, the substitution of paid for unpaid officials is in itself enough to constitute a serious revolution.

I regard the complete absence of unpaid officials in America as one of the most prominent signs of the absolute dominion that democracy exercises there. All public services, of whatever kind, are paid, so that everyone has not merely the right but also the means to perform them. Although in democratic States all citizens are qualified to hold positions in the government, not all are tempted to seek them. The number and abilities of the candidates are more likely to limit the electors’ choice than any conditions attached to candidacy.

In nations where the principle of election extends to every office in the State, no political career can properly be said to exist. Men are promoted as if by chance to the rank they hold, and they are by no means sure of keeping it. The consequence is that in tranquil times public offices offer few lures to ambition. In the United States the people who engage in the perplexities of political life are individuals of very moderate pretensions. The pursuit of wealth generally diverts men of great talents and great passions from the pursuit of power, and it very often happens that a man does not undertake to direct the fortunes of the State until he has found that he is incompetent to manage his own affairs. The vast number of very ordinary men in public office is as much due to these causes as to the democracy’s bad choices. In the United States I am not sure the people would elect men of superior abilities who sought its support, but it is certain that men of this kind do not come forward.
Arbitrary Power of Magistrates Under the Rule of the American Democracy
For what reason the arbitrary power of magistrates is greater in absolute monarchies and in democratic republics than in limited monarchies — The arbitrary power of the magistrates in New England.

In two different kinds of government the magistrates *a exercise a considerable degree of arbitrary power: under the absolute government of a single individual, and under that of a democracy. Nearly analogous causes produce this identical result.
a [ I use the word magistrates here in the widest sense it can have; I apply it to all the officers who are entrusted with the execution of the laws.]

In despotic States no citizen’s fortune is secure, and public officers are no safer than private individuals. The sovereign, who has under his control the lives, the property, and sometimes the honor of the men he employs, does not hesitate to give them great latitude of action, because he is convinced they will not use it against him. In despotic States the sovereign is so attached to the exercise of his power that he dislikes the constraint even of his own regulations, and he is quite content for his agents to follow a somewhat haphazard line of conduct, provided he is certain that their actions will never run counter to his wishes.

In democracies, since the majority has the right every year to remove from power the officers it has appointed, it has no reason to fear any abuse of their authority. Since the people can always make its wishes known to those who conduct the government, it prefers to leave them to make their own efforts rather than prescribe an invariable rule of conduct that would hamper both their activity and the people’s authority.

It may even be observed, on careful consideration, that under the rule of a democracy the arbitrary power of the magistrate must be still greater than in despotic States. In a despotic State the sovereign has the power to punish all the faults he learns of, but it would be vain for him to hope to learn of all those that are committed. In a democracy the sovereign power is not only supreme but present everywhere. American officials are, in fact, much more independent within the sphere of action the law marks out for them than any public officer in Europe. Very often they are simply told the object they are to accomplish, and the choice of means is left to their own discretion.

In New England, for instance, the selectmen of each township are required to draw up the list of persons who are to serve on the jury. The only rule laid down to guide their choice is that they must select citizens who have the right to vote and enjoy a fair reputation. *b In France the lives and liberties of the subjects would be thought endangered if a public officer of any kind were entrusted with so formidable a right. In New England the same magistrates are empowered to post the names of habitual drunkards in public houses and to forbid the inhabitants of the township from supplying them with liquor. *c Even the population of the most absolute monarchies would find a censorial power of this extreme kind revolting; here, however, it is accepted without difficulty.
b [ See the Act of February 27, 1813. “General Collection of the Laws of Massachusetts,” vol. ii. p. 331. It should be added that the jurors are afterward chosen by lot from these lists.]
c [ See Act of February 28, 1787. “General Collection of the Laws of Massachusetts,” vol. i. p. 302.]

Nowhere has so much been left by law to the arbitrary judgment of the magistrate as in democratic republics, because this arbitrary power brings no alarming consequences. It may even be said that the magistrate’s freedom grows as the right to vote is extended and as terms of office are shortened. Hence the great difficulty of converting a democratic republic into a monarchy. The magistrate stops being elected, but he keeps the rights and habits of an elected officer, which lead directly to despotism.

It is only in limited monarchies that the law, which prescribes the sphere in which public officers are to act, supervises all their measures. The reason is easy to see. In limited monarchies power is divided between the King and the people, and both have an interest in the stability of the magistrate. The King does not venture to place public officers under the people’s control, for fear they might be tempted to betray his interests. On the other hand, the people fears that if the magistrates were wholly dependent on the Crown, they might serve to oppress the country’s liberties. They cannot therefore be said to depend on either one or the other. The same cause that leads the king and the people to make public officers independent suggests the need for safeguards that keep that independence from encroaching on the authority of the former and the liberties of the latter. They therefore agree on the need to restrict the official to a line of conduct laid down in advance, and they both have an interest in confining him by certain regulations he cannot evade.
Instability of the Administration in the United States

In America the public acts of a community often leave fewer traces than the events of a family — Newspapers the only historical remains — The instability of the administration is harmful to the art of government.

Public men in America hold authority so briefly, and are so quickly lost again in the ever-changing population, that the acts of a community often leave fewer traces than the events of a private family. The public administration is, so to speak, oral and handed down by word of mouth. Little is written down, and that little is carried off forever by the slightest breeze, like the leaves of the Sibyl.

The only historical remains in the United States are the newspapers, but if one issue is missing, the chain of time is broken and the present is cut off from the past. I am convinced that in fifty years it will be harder to collect authentic documents about the social condition of Americans today than it is to find remains of the administration of France in the Middle Ages. And if the United States were ever invaded by barbarians, it would be necessary to turn to the history of other nations to learn anything about the people who now live there.

The instability of the administration has worked its way into the habits of the people. It even seems to suit the general taste, and no one cares what happened before his time. No methodical system is followed; no archives are kept; and no documents are gathered even when it would be very easy to do so. Where they exist, little store is set by them, and I have among my papers several original public documents that were given to me in answer to some of my inquiries. In America society seems to live from hand to mouth, like an army in the field. Nevertheless, the art of administration may undoubtedly be ranked as a science, and no science can be improved unless the discoveries and observations of successive generations are connected in the order in which they occur. One man, in the short span of his life, notices a fact; another conceives an idea; the first invents a means of carrying it out, the second reduces a truth to a fixed proposition; and mankind gathers the fruits of individual experience along its way and gradually builds up the sciences. But the people who conduct the administration in America can seldom teach each other anything, and when they take over the direction of society, they have only those attainments most widely spread in the community and no experience of their own. Democracy carried to its furthest limits is therefore harmful to the art of government, and for this reason it suits a people already practiced in administration better than a nation new to public affairs.

This remark, indeed, is not limited to the science of administration. Although a democratic government is founded on a very simple and natural principle, it always presupposes a high degree of culture and enlightenment in society. *d At first glance one might imagine it belongs to the earliest ages of the world, but closer observation will convince us that it could only come last in the sequence of human history.
d [ It hardly needs saying that I speak here of the democratic form of government as applied to a people, not merely to a tribe.]
Charges Levied by the State Under the Rule of the American Democracy

In all communities citizens can be divided into three classes — The habits of each class in directing public finances — Why public expenditure must tend to increase when the people governs — What makes the extravagance of a democracy less to be feared in America — Public expenditure under a democracy.

Before we can say whether a democratic form of government is economical or not, we must establish a suitable standard of comparison. The question would be easy to settle if we compared a democratic republic with an absolute monarchy. Public expenditure would turn out to be greater under the former than under the latter; this is true of all free States compared with those that are not free. It is certain that despotism ruins individuals by preventing them from producing wealth much more than by taking away the wealth they have produced; it dries up the source of riches while it usually respects acquired property. Freedom, on the contrary, produces far more benefits than it destroys, and nations favored with free institutions invariably find that their resources grow even faster than their taxes.
My present object is to compare free nations with one another and to point out the influence of democracy on the finances of a State.

Communities, like organic bodies, are subject to certain fixed rules in their formation that they cannot evade. They are made up of certain elements that are common to them at all times and in all circumstances. The people may always be mentally divided into three distinct classes. The first class consists of the wealthy; the second, of those in easy circumstances; and the third, of those who have little or no property and who live chiefly by the work they do for the two upper orders. The proportion of individuals in these three divisions may vary with the condition of society, but the divisions themselves can never be erased.

It is evident that each of these classes will exert, on the administration of the State’s finances, an influence peculiar to its own tendencies. If the first of the three holds the legislative power exclusively, it is likely to be free with public funds, because taxes levied on a large fortune only reduce the amount of superfluous enjoyment and are, in fact, little felt. If the second class has the power of making laws, it will certainly not be lavish with taxes, because nothing is so burdensome as a heavy tax levied on a small income. The government of the middle classes seems to me the most economical of free governments, though perhaps not the most enlightened and certainly not the most generous.

But let us now suppose that legislative authority is vested in the lowest orders. Two striking reasons show that expenditure will tend to increase, not decrease. Since the great majority of those who make the laws own no property that can be taxed, all the money spent for the community appears to be spent to their advantage, at no cost to themselves; and those who do own some small property readily find ways to arrange the taxes so that they burden the wealthy and benefit the poor, whereas the rich cannot take the same advantage when they are in possession of the government.
